summary: A humorous, tongue-in-cheek parody of grand academic papers about gigabit networks. It claims to propose a new paradigm for the standards track but is a joke. RFC 1217 is a reply in the same spirit.

eli5.summary: This is a joke paper that sounds very serious but is meant to make you laugh.

questions: what is ultra low speed networking
what is the alternating bit protocol
subtitle: An April 1st spoof that proposes Ultra Low Speed networking as the answer to gigabit hype.

tldr.problem: The joke's premise is that processing and memory costs fall faster than communication costs, which would supposedly bankrupt the internet community.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes a paradigm shift to Ultra Low Speed (ULS) networking at .01 uGbps, built on old protocols such as the alternating bit protocol.
tldr.outcome: It is an April 1st satire of gigabit-network hype and paradigm-shift language, with nothing meant to be implemented.

today: RFC 1216 is an Informational April 1st RFC with no replacement or update listed, and it was never meant as a real standard.

sections.title: An April 1st Joke Document
sections.content:
RFC 1216 is dated 1 April 1991 and is an April 1st joke document, written in the solemn style of a standards proposal. Its status note says it proposes "a new standard paradigm" for the IAB standardization track. The authors, "Poorer Richard" and "Prof. Kynikos", are playful names.

The target is the attention given to gigabit networks. The introduction praises small, largely unfunded research efforts that deal with technical problems within the constraints of economic science.
sections.eli5: It is a silly paper dressed up as a serious one, making fun of how excited people were about super fast networks.

sections.title: The Economics Argument
sections.content:
The text cites a projection that the cost per bit and per MIP will fall 99% per decade, while the cost per bps falls 90% per decade. It argues that this 9% difference, compounded, will bankrupt the internet community unless a paradigm shift takes place.

The joke is the reasoning: more processing power creates demand for bandwidth but does nothing to pay for it, so the proposed fix is to go slower, not faster.
sections.eli5: The authors say computers get cheap faster than wires do, so the answer is to use slower networks. It is funny because it is backwards.

sections.title: The Ultra Low Speed Paradigm
sections.content:
The ULS shift focuses on end-to-end datagrams and virtual circuit services in the .01 uGbps region. It claims individual circuits could cost under $.03/month. Suggested applications include low priority facsimile with three-hour delivery, tracking glaciers, the US postal service and contracting for research. Scaled further, it adds gravity wave detectors, the Italian postal service and the Congressional budget process.

Technically, since "Gigabit networks require new protocols", ULS will need old protocols. The alternating bit protocol is a leading contender, with 1 bit sequence numbers. It also says "Bad news travel fast", so ULS gives preferential treatment to good news.
sections.eli5: Their plan is a network so slow it is almost like sending letters. They say that is perfect for things that are not in a hurry.

sections.title: Problems and Conclusions
sections.content:
The RFC lists problems: ULS protocols all incorporate slow-start, lower data rates mean fewer errors, and small headers shrink the header/data ratio. The result is "creeping efficiency", which pushes away from the proper ULS operating point. Proposed palliatives include Forward Error Insertion (FEI), negative window scaling factors, new protocol layers and multiple presentation layers.

The conclusion reads: the road to Ultra Low Speed technology is long, slow, and easy. The memo's Security Considerations say security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: The only trouble they find is that things might get too good and too fast again, so they suggest ways to keep them slow.

references.text: Lynch, W., "Reliable full-duplex file transmission over half-duplex telephone lines", CACM, pp. 407-410, June 1968.
